Euro FAQs
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

EUDR implementation briefing
- EUDR compliance begins in December 2026 for larger companies
- Further EUDR simplifications appear unlikely despite continued political opposition
- Industry support remains strong, though some companies seek changes
- A third delay remains possible but implementation appears more likely
- Further delays could undermine EUDR and EU credibility
The European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) is on the horizon.
The deadline is fast approaching: larger companies will need to comply with the law from 30 December 2026, with the deadline for smaller companies coming six months later on 30 June 2027.
The law has seen two delays and several simplifications since it was first proposed.
Now that we’re on the home stretch, what are the chances that the landmark law will see last-minute changes, alterations or delays? Will it get over the line as planned?
The state of the EUDR
The EUDR has been through many shifts. In 2024, the regulation was delayed, which was followed in 2025 by a second year-long delay. Then, earlier this year, a simplification package was released, easing compliance burdens for certain operators.
Yet in the view of Bill Cordingley, barrister at the law firm Browne Jacobson, we have now arrived at the “definitive version” of the EUDR, or at least close to it.
“The Commission has already implemented a substantial simplification exercise and argues that, as a result, compliance costs have been significantly reduced.”
If there are any further changes, he suggests, they are more likely to focus on practical implementation issues, guidance and administrative burdens, rather than reworking the traceability and due diligence requirements themselves.
Further simplifications are “unlikely”, suggests Nicole Polsterer, sustainable consumption and production campaigner at the NGO Fern. Fern is not aware of a sizeable group within the European Parliament pushing for more simplifications.
Opposition to the EUDR from industry
The industry is broadly supportive of the EUDR, with companies such as Barry Callebaut and Ferrero showing strong support.
However, opposition has been voiced from some quarters, with snacking giant Mondelēz International and coffee company Lavazza traditionally pushing for simplifications.
According to NGO Global Witness, Mondelēz has been lobbying the US government, with CEO Dirk Van de Put meeting US Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder to push to weaken the law.
According to Global Witness, Mondelēz has also been executing a “pan-European lobbying strategy”, targeting conservative MEPs in Brussels as well as meeting with governments in France, Germany, Ireland and Luxembourg.
In response to Global Witness’s piece, a Mondelēz spokesperson said that the company “fully supports the objectives of the EU Deforestation Regulation and remains committed to deforestation-free supply chains and responsible sourcing across our operations and value chain”.
Opposition to the EUDR from governments
The EUDR also faces opposition from the US, with Puzder describing it as “textbook overregulation”, which will “impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit”.
The US has asked for further simplifications for low-risk countries, explains Fern’s Polsterer.
Yet Cordingley does not believe that, at this stage, opposition from the US could lead to further changes. On the one hand, “external political pressures could still have some influence on the debate”, and concerns from trading partners such as the US could reinforce existing trends towards deregulation and attempts to rejuvenate competitiveness.
On the other, “the EUDR remains one of the EU’s flagship environmental measures and is not far off coming into force and so I do not think pressure from climate-sceptical governments alone is likely to be enough to derail it altogether”.
Opposition to the EUDR from the European Parliament
Then there is opposition from within the European Parliament. Groups such as the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) have long been in favour of simplifications and revisions to the EUDR.
“Internally we know there is now a sizeable political constituency within the Parliament that would weaken parts of the regulation given the opportunity,” says Cordingley.
Yet a substantial coalition of MEPs still back the regulation and oppose any significant rollback. While Cordingley sees the potential for some pressure to further moderate the rules, he does not believe that there is an obvious Parliamentary majority to dismantle the regime entirely.
Could there be a third delay?
It would be “foolish” to rule out the possibility of a third delay, says Cordingley. EU Member States are still lobbying for further simplification and postponement. Political resistance has far from disappeared.
At the same time, the European Commission has presented the simplification package as addressing the concerns of industry and Member States, he says. It has repeatedly stressed the current timetable.
“I think implementation in December 2026 remains more likely than another delay but I can’t fully discount the political picture shifting quickly in the weeks ahead.”
How could further simplifications impact the law?
If more changes were introduced to the law, it would significantly weaken its credibility, suggests Tina Schneider, director of forest governance and policy at the organisation World Resources Institute (WRI).
“Moving the goalposts again would undermine confidence in the regulatory process and raise serious questions about the EU’s commitment to delivering on the environmental goals the law was designed to achieve.”
A third delay would weaken the credibility not only of the EUDR but of the EU itself, suggests Fern’s Polsterer. She suggests that if there is a delay, it may be blamed on the IT system or on food security.
Right now, things are looking good for the EUDR. But in the past, events have moved quickly. While opposition to the regulation remains, further simplifications, or even a further delay, cannot be completely ruled out.

Russia would have to go "all-in" if it were to launch an incursion into Estonia, an expert has said. There has been speculation over recent days at to whether the Kremlin could orchestrate a takeover of part of the Baltic country. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggested that Russian agents would take over major buildings in Narva. Experts also pointed out that long-range drones could be launched from Russia.
Merili Arjakas, a research fellow at The International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) - a think tank in Estonia specialising in security, defence and foreign policy issues - and the editor-in-chief of foreign policy magazine Diplomaatia, told The Express: "Russia cannot expect that any such attack against Estonia or the Baltic states will remain limited, as if the European states had not learned anything from the annexation in Crimea and the war in Donbas, which led to the full-scale invasion eight years later.
"That is not to say that Russia is not an aggressive power or that Putin does not dream of the collapse of NATO. Rather, any incursion will face a strong and immediate response from us and our partners."
A small-scale operation would not be sufficient, Ms Arjakas suggested.
She said: "Therefore, if I were Russia and I wanted to attack Estonia or the Baltics, I would go all-in, not think that any limited incursion to Narva or to other places would be enough.
"Fortunately for us, Russia has so far been careful to not create conditions for a large-scale confrontation with NATO. Its tolerance of such risk has certainly increased as they carry out more attacks that fall below the threshold for triggering Article 5.
"However, such asymmetric escalation is also characteristic of a weaker party, one that still deems it too risky to use conventional means."
Estonia is "taking the threat seriously", the specialist added, while also pointing major NATO weaknesses.
"Our defence budget for 2026 is 5.4% of GDP (€2.4billion), with major spending on ammunition, medium-range air defence, HIMARS, UAVs, anti-tank systems and territorial defence," Ms Arjakas said.
"Similar investments have been done by Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, while Finland has long been a shining example of a country armed to the teeth and prepared to fight.
"There are vulnerabilities - particularly in defence against missiles and drones, as well as in terms of reinforcement and logistics in the event of a full-scale invasion. But these are not vulnerabilities unique to Estonia or the eastern flank; rather, they are shared by all NATO countries except the US.
"Our best way of avoiding a NATO-Russia war, whether it erupts here or elsewhere, is still to support Ukraine so the aggressor does not prevail there. Ukraine keeps Russian forces and resources tied down and degrades Russian military capacity, thereby not only fighting for its own survival and sovereignty but also acting as a shield for Europe."

The United Kingdom government is actively evaluating the imposition of import tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, marking a significant potential shift in post-Brexit trade strategy. The move is reportedly being considered to align British policy with the European Union, thereby strengthening the UK’s case for inclusion in the bloc’s forthcoming industrial protection legislation designed to shield domestic manufacturing from subsidized foreign competition.
According to industry reports and diplomatic sources, the EU has directly raised the question of tariff alignment with UK officials during ongoing negotiations surrounding the "Made in Europe" framework, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). The IAA represents a cornerstone of the European Commission’s strategy to revitalize the continent's industrial base, requiring manufacturers to procure components locally and imposing strict conditions on third countries seeking access to its protected supply chains. Brussels maintains that for the UK to qualify for inclusion in this scheme and benefit from a level playing field, it must mirror the punitive tariffs of up to 45 percent that the EU levied on Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles in October 2024.
Currently, the UK stands as a notable outlier among major Western economies in its refusal to enact blanket import taxes on Chinese automotive products. While the United States has effectively shut out Chinese EVs through aggressive trade barriers, and the EU has implemented targeted anti-subsidy duties following a lengthy investigation, the previous UK administration maintained a more open market approach. The prevailing argument in Westminster has historically been that Britain does not require the same protective trade barriers as the EU, largely because the UK does not suffer from the same massive trade deficit in goods that Brussels is struggling to contain.
However, the risk assessment within Whitehall has reportedly evolved. Senior government sources indicate that the impending implementation of the EU's Industrial Accelerator Act poses a direct threat to the British automotive sector. The UK car industry remains deeply integrated with European supply chains, and the EU remains the largest export market for finished British vehicles and components. If the UK is excluded from the "Made in Europe" provisions due to its failure to impose equivalent tariffs on Chinese imports, domestic manufacturers could face severe competitive disadvantages, potentially leading to production shifts and job losses within the UK.
Implementing such tariffs, however, is not a straightforward administrative decision. Any unilateral imposition of import duties would likely trigger a hostile response from Beijing, complicating broader diplomatic and trade relations at a time when the UK is seeking to stabilize its post-Brexit international partnerships. Furthermore, establishing legally defensible tariffs requires a rigorous process through the World Trade Organization (WTO). The EU’s own investigation into state subsidies within the Chinese EV supply chain took 13 months to conclude before duties could be lawfully applied. The UK would need to conduct its own trade remedy investigation, gathering evidence of market distortion and economic injury to domestic producers, a process that could delay the implementation of any new duties well into the future.
The political dynamics surrounding this decision are equally complex. The current government has previously positioned itself as pragmatic regarding Chinese investment, viewing it as a potential driver of economic growth rather than solely a systemic risk to British manufacturing. A pivot toward protectionist tariffs would represent a stark departure from that rhetoric, signaling a prioritization of domestic industrial security over consumer access to low-cost green technology. Consumer advocates and environmental groups have previously warned that tariffs on Chinese EVs could artificially inflate vehicle prices, potentially slowing the UK’s transition to zero-emission transport and complicating the achievement of national climate targets.
European industry leaders, particularly within the automotive and chemicals sectors, have lobbied intensely for a unified front against the influx of heavily subsidized Chinese exports. They argue that without coordinated tariffs, European and British manufacturers cannot compete on price, regardless of their technological advancements. The UK’s participation in the IAA’s supply chain requirements would mandate that a significant percentage of vehicle components be sourced from within the UK or the EU, a stipulation designed to rebuild regional industrial capacity and reduce reliance on Asian supply networks.
The Industrial Accelerator Act encompasses strategic industries beyond automotive, including green hydrogen and advanced chemicals. For the UK’s chemical sectors, exclusion from the IAA’s preferential treatment could divert foreign direct investment toward EU member states. Multinational corporations planning new gigafactories may bypass the UK if it cannot offer guaranteed access to the protected European market. Furthermore, imposing anti-subsidy duties under WTO rules requires the UK’s Trade Remedies Authority (TRA) to initiate a formal probe, demonstrating a link between foreign financial contributions and material injury to domestic industry. This evidentiary burden ensures tariffs are grounded in rigorous economic analysis, though the process invites intense scrutiny from both Beijing and Brussels.
The environmental implications present a significant policy paradox. While the UK is committed to phasing out internal combustion engines, the affordability of EVs remains a barrier to mass adoption. Chinese manufacturers leverage state-backed supply chains to produce EVs at a fraction of European costs. Imposing a 45 percent tariff would pass costs onto consumers, potentially stalling the EV market and undermining carbon reduction commitments. Policymakers are exploring alternative mechanisms, such as localized battery manufacturing incentives, to offset the price differential without resorting to blunt import taxes.
As the deadline for the finalization of the Industrial Accelerator Act approaches, the pressure on Whitehall to declare its position is intensifying. The outcome of these deliberations will not only dictate the price of cars on British driveways but will fundamentally reshape the UK’s integration into European industrial policy for decades to come.

By Felix Armstrong
Wall Street eked out gains on Monday’s market open, as oil prices and borrowing costs stayed put after rising late last week.

The average five-year fixed mortgage rate has broken the six per cent mark for the first time in three years after a fresh raft of lenders hiked prices.
The typical five-year agreement has hit six per cent, according to Moneyfacts, while the average two-year is a whisker behind at 5.98 per cent. It is the highest since September 2023 for the five-year and December 2023 for the two-year.
Barclays has hiked selected fixed rates on four occasions. HSBC, Lloyds, Nationwide, Natwest, Santander and TSB have all made three rounds of increases.
“Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers,” Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts, said.

According to an analysis of the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, super-rich UK residents worth a combined $160bn (£121bn) have either left or loosened ties with UK since 2024 after the Labour government announced a succession of measures clamping down on wealth.
The figure represents more than half of all billionaire wealth in the UK, the analysis said, and comprises the fortunes of a slew of high-profile entrepreneurs including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal, Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and shipping magnate John Fredriksen.

articles.title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis - BBC
articles.summary: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis  BBCThe right and wrong lessons to learn from Spain’s housing crisis  Financial TimesSpain's lefty government evicted an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years and thousands of protesters took the streets  FortuneSpain’s New Protest Movement Is Putting Class Center Stage  JacobinNearly 500,000 people protest in Madrid over Spain's housing crisis  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.
About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.
"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.
The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.
Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.
Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.
Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.
Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.
One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.
Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".
Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.
One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."
Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.
Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".
Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.
On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".
It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.
The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.
It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

articles.title: Iran insists it controls Hormuz as rial hits record low and exports dry up - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Iran insists it controls Hormuz as rial hits record low and exports dry up  Euronews.comIran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met  Reuters‘Flames Will Engulf Everyone’: Iran Warns against New War, Threatens US Interests  Palestine ChronicleIran reviews US response to seven-day proposal as officials debate next steps  Iran InternationalIran-US war live: Tehran threatens to keep Hormuz shut until US meets conditions  The I...
articles.full_text:
Iran's military insisted it retained full control of Hormuz and the foreign minister said the strait could reopen within seven days if Tehran's conditions were met, after US Treasury Secretary Bessent said Iran had not loaded a single barrel of crude onto tankers in September.
Iran's military said on Monday it retained full control over the Strait of Hormuz despite changes in US tactics, as the rial fell to record lows, the oil minister resigned and Washington claimed Tehran had not exported a single barrel of crude in September.
"All movements (in Hormuz) are under the control of the armed forces of the Islamic Republic," Brigadier General Aziz Jafari, commander of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Joint Air Defence Headquarters, said Monday.
Hours before Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad's resignation was announced, he said in a video released by Iranian media that revenue from oil already sold would be collected and the process would continue.
His departure was officially attributed to "family and personal matters," although speculation has mounted that exports have fallen to a level that no longer covers state financial needs.
"Iran did not load any crude oil onto tankers in September. The Trump administration is cutting off the Iranian regime's most vital source of revenue," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote on X on Thursday.
Pezeshkian had acknowledged in August that the blockade was disrupting exports. "We used to sell oil; now we cannot sell it," he said. The new acting oil minister pledged to maximise production and continue exports through new strategies.
Ship-tracking company Kpler recorded crude exports from the region excluding Iran at between 19.5 and 22.5 million barrels per day in the final week of September, above the pre-war regional average of 18 million barrels per day.
The euro broke through 300,000 tomans on Iran's informal market, while the US dollar hit a record 270,000 tomans — more than double its level at the start of this year, when it stood at around 135,000 tomans.
At the time of the 1979 Islamic revolution, the US dollar was worth approximately 7 tomans. The rial is Iran's official currency; one toman equals ten rials.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or the Gulf of Aden since 2 October.
Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of the armed forces general staff, warned international organisations and responded to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's visit to the United Arab Emirates.
"If for any reason Israel once again commits a miscalculation and starts another war, the fury of the armed forces will shatter its hopes and dreams," he said. "Be aware that if a new war against Iran begins, its flames will engulf everyone."
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told foreign ambassadors in Tehran that the conflict had no military solution. "If our enemies once again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be firmer than before," he said.
"Only negotiations founded on justice and fairness can offer a way to end this conflict." He said the Strait could be fully reopened and shipping restored within seven days if Tehran's conditions were met and hostile measures lifted.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran had received proposals from Washington through intermediaries but would not accept one-sided demands.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and definitive, and until our seven conditions based on the Islamabad memorandum are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened," Ghalibaf said.

Facial recognition technology could mean Britons no longer need to show their passports at e-gates when they fly back to the UK.
Passengers would still need to travel with their passport in order to check in and board planes but new “contactless borders” are expected to be introduced at Birmingham and East Midlands airports in the coming weeks in an effort to reduce queues, it has been reported.
This would then be extended to all e-gates, already in operation at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted airports, by early next year, according to The Times.
The system is currently expected to work for British passport holders, but could be extended to other nationalities with biometric passports allowed to use e-gates, the publication reported.
Phil Douglas, the director general of Border Force, told the paper that the move could speed up border control by 25 per cent.
“It will mean we have a more secure border and a much faster transit through the airport. It’s quicker, it’s more modern, it’s more secure,” he said.
The paper reported that the current process, which aimed to speed up border checks, often was held up because of problems with the chip on the passport being dirty or even people who didn’t place their passports in the machine correctly.
The system would see a gallery of passport photos of British passengers arriving that day transmitted by each airline to Border Control.
Those not recognised by the e-gate they will be asked to scan their passport, according to the report. If that fails, they would then be directed to a Border Force officer at a manned desk.
It’s the latest proposal for facial recognition technology which has so far been deployed by the police forces, Sainsbury’s and Revolut.
Privacy activists have warned that the technology is error-ridden and risks the UK becoming a surveillance state as there are no laws in place to protect citizen privacy.
Sainsbury’s was forced to apologise after a 42-year-old man was wrongly identified as an offende. Staff approached him, asked him to leave and took his shopping in January.
Big Brother Watch has reported 80 per cent of people misidentified by facial recognition in London in 2025 were Black, warning the technology discriminates against women and people of colour.
Already, the Metropolitan Police has used the technology to monitor Oxford Street, tube stations and Notting Hill carnival.
The biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner warned in May that the technology was not “fool proof” and could land forces in legal difficulty as “misidentified” members of the public could sue the police for breaching their fundamental rights.
Revolut now allows customers to pay with a biometric face scan, linked to their app, which meant customers did not need a phone or bank card to make a payment.
The Independent has contacted the Home Office, Birmingham and East Midlands Airport for comment.
